newsitem.title: UK: EIU lowers world 96/97 cocoa deficit to 85,000T.
newsitem.headline: EIU lowers world 96/97 cocoa deficit to 85,000T.

text.p: The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) on Tuesday lowered its 1996/97 world cocoa deficit estimate to 85,000 tonnes from 200,000 previously due to higher-than-expected production.
In 1995/96, cocoa posted a supply surplus of 160,000 tonnes.
In its third quarter 1997 world commodity forecasts (food, feedstuffs and beverages), the EIU put the supply deficit at 73,000 tonnes in 1997/98 and 18,000 in 1998/99.
The London-based think tank said the downward revision in the 1996/97 deficit followed substantially higher-than-expected production in Ivory Coast.
It now put this season's Ivorian crop at 1.14 million tonnes (1.0 million previously), but still down from 1995/96's record 1.2 million.
It also revised upward estimate for the 1997/98 crop to 1.10 million from 1.0 million previously.
The EIU also raised current crop estimates for Ghana and Nigeria but cut those for Brazil and Malaysia.

"The net effect is a fairly hefty rise in our global figure to 2.7 million tonnes (previously 2.59 million), which compares with the latest forecasts of the ICCO (International Cocoa Organisation) and (UK trade house) E D & F Man of 2.68 million and 2.61 million tonnes respectively," it said.
The EIU also revised upward its estimate for cocoa stock-to-consumption ratio to 42.8 percent by the end of 1998/99 from 34.3 percent -- the lowest for 13 years -- previously.
It said the outlook for prices was therefore less rosy.
"But because of ICCO buffer stock sales will end in 1998 and global inventories are still falling, prices will continue to rise."
It also said its production figures for Ivory Coast did not take into account possible government measures to limit supplies in order to boost prices.
"Also to be considered is the fate of the large commercial stocks of 300,000 tonnes held by one trade house," the EIU said.
"If our fundamental analysis is correct, the scope for using these holdings to squeeze the market upwards will be substantially lower...," it said. -- Jalil Hamid, London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
